{{Short description|Bulgarian astronomer}}
'''Dimitar D. Sasselov''' ({{langx|bg|Димитър Д. Съселов}}; born 1961) is a [[Bulgarians|Bulgarian]] [[astronomer]] based in the [[United States]]. He is a Professor of Astronomy at [[Harvard University]] and director of the Harvard Origins of Life Initiative.<ref name="nasa">{{cite web |title=Dimitar Sasselov Bio |url=http://www.nasa.gov/pdf/415119main_Dimitar%20Sasselov%20Bio.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100209213858/http://www.nasa.gov/pdf/415119main_Dimitar%20Sasselov%20Bio.pdf |archive-date=2010-02-09 |accessdate=21 July 2010 |publisher=[[NASA]]}}</ref> In 2002, Sasselov led a team that discovered the most distant planet in the [[Milky Way]] known at the time.<ref name="harvardgazette">{{cite news |url=http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2004/10.14/03-sasselov.html |title=Finding the hot planets beyond our solar system |last=Cromie |first=William J. |date=2004-10-14 |work=Harvard Gazette |publisher=Harvard University |accessdate=21 July 2010 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100726122641/http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2004/10.14/03-sasselov.html |archivedate=26 July 2010 }}</ref>

Sasselov was born in [[Bulgaria]] to a scientific family. His father was an [[architect]] and his Greek mother was a [[horticulturist]]. He developed a liking for astronomy at an early age and would observe the [[moons of Jupiter]] by means of a small [[telescope]].<ref name="harvardgazette" /> Sasselov finished a primary school in [[Nesebar]] and a high school in [[Burgas]].<ref name="nauka">{{cite news|url=http://www.democrit.com/the_news.php?n=201 |title=Планета, открита с участието на BG-учен |date=2003-03-21 |work=Наука |publisher=Демокрит |language=Bulgarian |accessdate=21 July 2010 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110709011849/http://www.democrit.com/the_news.php?n=201 |archivedate=9 July 2011 }}</ref>

In the 1980s, Sasselov continued his study of astronomy at the [[Sofia University]]'s Faculty of Physics. After he published a paper in international [[scientific journal]]s, he was invited by the [[University of Toronto]], who offered him a scholarship. However, Sasselov was not granted an exit visa by the Bulgarian authorities. He acquired a doctorate in physics from Sofia University in 1988;<ref name="nasa" /><ref name="edge">{{cite web |url=http://www.edge.org/3rd_culture/bios/sasselov.html |title=Dimitar D. Sasselov |publisher=Edge |accessdate=21 July 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100731011959/http://www.edge.org/3rd_culture/bios/sasselov.html |archive-date=31 July 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> shortly thereafter, with the [[collapse of the Soviet Union]] and the communist regimes in Eastern Europe, Sasselov had the chance to eventually continue his work at the University of Toronto. In 1990, he earned his doctorate in astronomy there.<ref name="nasa" /><ref name="harvardgazette" /><ref name="edge" />

In 1991, Sasselov joined the [[Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics|Center for Astrophysics {{!}} Harvard & Smithsonian]].<ref name="harvardgazette" /> He has been a Harvard professor since 1998.<ref name="edge" /> In 2002, Sasselov and his team sighted [[OGLE-TR-56b]], a planet in the constellation [[Sagittarius (constellation)|Sagittarius]] that was the farthest planet from the [[Earth]] discovered until then.<ref name="harvardgazette" /><ref name="harvardgazette2">{{cite news |url=http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2003/01.16/01-ogle.html |title=New, far-out planet is discovered |last=Cromie |first=William J. |date=2003-01-16 |work=Harvard Gazette |publisher=Harvard University |accessdate=21 July 2010 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090827072608/http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2003/01.16/01-ogle.html |archivedate=27 August 2009 }}</ref> In his search for planets, he employs novel methods that can potentially detect planets similar to Earth, and he co-operates with [[NASA]]'s [[Kepler Mission]]. Sasselov's other research focuses on the interaction between [[radiation]] and [[matter]].<ref name="nasa" />
